findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is and what makes it different. This works well.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: A link to the next step sits right in the header, so the reader doesn't have to scroll through the study to find out what to do.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header)

findings.text: This is the page someone gets at Athena's own web address, but after the opening it is all about firstmate, a project the newcomer probably hasn't heard of. Someone who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on it and many screens on firstmate's internals.
findings.source:
Athena explains how firstmate handles work

; sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions", "Claims and sources"

findings.text: The page says why the study exists, but not why a newcomer would want Athena. It never links this ability to the main job it described: turning a request into a code change. The lede says Athena records what each step costs, but nothing on the page shows that.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The install steps leave out how to get the checkout and what is needed first, such as tools or model API keys. They also don't say what `athena ask` produces. A newcomer would have to go to the GitHub repo before they could act.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Some firstmate terms are used but never defined, even though the page has a glossary. These include "open captain call", "endpoint", "durable record" and "captain-held inventory", which makes the dense transition cards hard for a newcomer to follow.
findings.source: "teardown reopens it instead of closing it" / "A stale wake shows the worker is stuck" / "its captain-held inventory is verified"

findings.text: "green" is defined as the opposite of "red", but "red" is only defined in the next entry. So the first definitions a reader meets refer forward to terms they haven't seen yet.
findings.source: Words used first: "green — A PR that is not red" (listed before "red")

findings.text: This uses Athena's internal terms ("job", "recorded boundary", "marked read") without explaining them. A newcomer can't tell what this limit means.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The page refers to a `studies/` folder without saying which repository it is in. That gives the newcomer nothing to act on.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: Every statement can be traced to an exact line at a pinned commit. This shows Athena's value directly, for readers who get that far.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
